Authors: Ali Davoudian, Liu Chen, and Mengchi 
Liu

1. Concrete Experience 
A. Summary of the Paper 
“A Survey on NoSQL Stores” by Davoudian, Chen, and Liu (2018) addresses the 
difficulties that traditional relational database management systems (RDBMS) face when 
handling the scale, velocity, and variety of data generated by modern web, mobile, and 
cloud applications. The authors explain that the rigid, predefined schema of relational 
systems makes them costly to evolve, difficult to scale horizontally across commodity 
servers, and prone to availability problems when distributed ACID transactions are used 
across many nodes (Davoudian et al., 2018). These limitations gave rise to NoSQL ( “Not 
Only SQL”) stores, a newer generation of database technology designed to give web-scale 
applications the high availability, horizontal scalability, and flexible, schema -less data 
handling that RDBMSs struggle to provide. 
The purpose of the survey is not to declare NoSQL a replacement for relational databases, 
but to organize the large and fragmented landscape of NoSQL systems around four 
fundamental, non-orthogonal design decisions that every distributed data store must make: 
the data model used to represent information, the consistency model used to coordinate 
replicas, the strategy used to partition data across nodes, and the trade -offs described by 
the CAP theorem. For each of these four design dimensions the authors cla ssify the 
available strategies, describe their strengths and drawbacks, and illustrate them using real 
academic and industrial systems such as Amazon Dynamo, Google Bigtable, Apache 
Cassandra, MongoDB, and Neo4j. 
The scope of the paper is broad, covering key -value, wide-column, document, and graph 
data models; consistency models ranging from strong linearizability to eventual and causal 
consistency; static and workload -aware partitioning strategies; and the CAP/PAC ELC 
trade-offs that shape how distributed stores are engineered. The paper closes by identifying 
open research challenges that the NoSQL community still needs to address, making it a 
useful reference point for anyone choosing or designing a data store for a large -scale 
application. 
B. Key Findings 
• NoSQL stores share common characteristics: schema -less or flexible data models, 
relaxed (weak) consistency in place of strict ACID guarantees, heavy use of data 
duplication and “aggregates” to avoid costly joins, and designs that are cluster - and 
datacenter-friendly for horizontal scaling (Davoudian et al., 2018). 
• Four main NoSQL data models exist (key-value, wide-column, document, and graph), 
each suited to different access patterns; for example, key -value stores fit single -key 
lookups while graph stores fit deeply connected data. 
• Consistency models range from strong guarantees such as linearizability and 
serializability to weaker models such as eventual consistency, causal consistency, and 
per-object timeline consistency; weaker models trade strict correctness for lower 
latency and higher availability. 
• Data partitioning can be key -oriented (range -based, simple hashing, consistent 
hashing, hyperspace hashing) or traversal -oriented for graphs, and can be static or 
workload-aware to correct load imbalance across nodes. 
• The CAP theorem shows that a distributed store can guarantee at most two of 
Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at once; because network partitions 
cannot be avoided in practice, most NoSQL stores are designed to sacrifice strict 
consistency (AP systems) or availability during a partition (CP systems). • NoSQL stores gain scalability and flexibility at a cost: most lack a standard query 
language, offer limited support for multi-key transactions, and shift more responsibility 
for data modeling and consistency handling onto the application developer. 
C. Techniques / Research Approach Used 
“A Survey on NoSQL Stores” is a survey and taxonomy paper rather than an experimental 
or empirical study. Davoudian et al. (2018) do not run new experiments or benchmarks of 
their own; instead, they synthesize and organize existing research and system 
documentation. Their method is to identify four foundational, non -orthogonal design 
dimensions of distributed data stores and, for each dimension, build a classification of the 
strategies used in practice. They then select a representative set of academic systems (e.g., 
Amazon Dynamo, Scalaris, Spinnaker) and industrial systems (e.g., Cassandra, MongoDB, 
Neo4j, Google Bigtable) to exemplify each strategy, describing how a real system 
implements it and what trade -offs result. Throughout, the authors combine text ual 
explanation with conceptual diagrams (such as data -model illustrations and architecture 
figures) and comparison tables that summarize the strengths, limitations, and representative 
systems for each category. This qualitative, taxonomy-driven approach suits a fast-moving 
and fragmented field such as NoSQL, where the goal is to give readers a structured mental 
model rather than a numerical performance comparison. 
D. Figures / Data Found Most Interesting 
Because the paper does not present an original experimental dataset, the most useful 
elements are its classification tables and conceptual diagrams rather than empirical figures. 
Table 2, “Comparison of NoSQL Data Models,” is especially useful because it lines up the 
fit scenarios, strengths, and limitations of key -value, wide-column, document, and graph 
stores side by side, making it easy to reason about which model suits which application. 
Figure 2, which shows how Facebook’s Inbox Search, McGraw-Hill Education’s learning 
portal, and Facebook’s social graph actually used the wide -column, document, and graph 
data models respectively, is also valuable because it grounds the abstract data -model 
discussion in real production use cases. Table 5, which categorizes representative NoSQL 
stores according to which CAP guarantee they sacrifice, gives a concrete way to connect 
the abstract CAP theorem to specific, well-known systems such as Cassandra, MongoDB, 
and Google Bigtable (Davoudian et al., 2018). 
2. Reflective Observation 
A. Personal Reflection 
The part of the paper I found most interesting was the discussion of the CAP theorem and 
the more practical PACELC framework it references (Davoudian et al., 2018). Before 
reading this survey, I understood the CAP theorem only in its simplified textbook fo rm: a 
system can be consistent, available, or partition tolerant, but not all three at once. What 
surprised me was learning that “availability” and “consistency” have precise, almost 
idealized definitions in CAP that do not always match how available or consistent a system 
feels in practice, and that many real systems, such as Yahoo Pnuts and Google Bigtable, 
cannot be placed cleanly into a single CAP category because they offer different guarantees 
for different types of operations. Reading this survey expanded my understanding of NoSQL databases considerably. Before 
the reading, I thought of “NoSQL” mainly as “databases that don’t use tables,” associated 
chiefly with document stores such as MongoDB. The paper made clear that NoSQL is
